title: Plastic Gift Cards vs Paper Gift Certificates for the Holidays
excerpt: Plastic gift cards look like a real present and last in a wallet. Paper gift certificates cost less and are numbered for tracking. Here's how Columbus spas, salons and restaurants can choose.
author: David Stein
featuredAlt: Fanned stack of glossy plastic gift cards with a red and cream wave design on a cafe counter beside a card reader
content:
If you run a spa, a salon or a restaurant in Columbus, sell gift cards this holiday season, and pick the format by how your customers give them. Plastic gift cards look like a real present and survive months in a wallet, so they work best when people buy them to hand to someone else. Paper gift certificates cost less and can be numbered in order, so they work best when you want a simple way to track every one you sell. Plenty of businesses do both.

I print plastic gift cards and paper gift certificates in Columbus with your logo on them. Below is how to choose between them, what to put on the card, and how to set up the counter so the cards actually sell.

Why gift cards matter in December

A gift card is a sale today and a new customer later. Someone buys one for a friend, and the friend walks in for the first time with the bill already paid. For a spa or salon, that first visit is often how a regular starts. For a restaurant, it fills a table in January, when most people are staying home.

The holidays are the big season for this. The earlier the cards are at your register, the more weeks you have to sell them. If you're reading this late in the season, cards still sell all the way up to the last shopping days, and again in the new year for birthdays and Valentine's Day.

Plastic gift cards: when they fit

Plastic gift cards are the standard credit card size, 2.125 x 3.375, the same as the cards already in someone's wallet. Rounded corners make them look even more like a bank card. They're waterproof and won't tear, so a card that sits in a purse until March still looks good when it comes back.

Plastic is the right pick when:

  • Most of your gift cards are bought as presents. A plastic card in a small envelope looks like a gift on its own.
  • You sell the same values over and over, like a set dollar amount or a named service.
  • You want something that keeps selling all year, not only in December.

You can choose white, frosted or clear plastic. White prints color the way paper does. Frosted lets some light through. Clear shows whatever is behind it, so the design has to be planned around the see-through parts. For most spas and restaurants, white is the safe choice.

One thing to check first: the cards I print are printed plastic, with no magnetic stripe. If your register or booking system needs a stripe or a barcode to load a balance, tell me which system you use before we print, and I'll check what it takes.

Paper gift certificates: when they fit

Paper gift certificates are printed on heavy card stock and numbered in order. That number is the whole tracking system. Write it in a log when you sell one, note the amount, and cross it off when it comes back. At any point you can see which certificates are still out there.

Paper is the right pick when:

  • You want to spend less per piece.
  • Values change a lot, so staff write in the amount or the service by hand.
  • You don't have a register system that tracks card balances, and a numbered log is what you'll actually keep up with.
  • You want a larger piece with room for a handwritten note and the recipient's name.

A certificate tucked into a branded envelope still feels like a gift. It just won't last in a wallet the way plastic does.

What to put on the card

Keep the front simple: your logo, your colors and maybe one line like "A gift for you." The back does the work. Most businesses include:

  • The value, or a blank line for it.
  • Your address, phone number and website.
  • How to book or redeem it, like "Book online or call to schedule."
  • A short line with your terms. Ohio and federal rules cover gift card expiration dates and fees, so check those before you print anything about them.
  • A number or a blank for one, if you're tracking by hand.

Send me your logo and the values you sell. I'll lay out the card, and you approve a proof before anything prints. On a first order, design and setup are free. Plastic card runs start at 100 cards, and reorders cost less once your file is set up.

Setting up the counter so they sell

Gift cards sell when people see them. A box of cards behind the register doesn't do much. A few things that help:

  • Put a small display at checkout with a sample card and the values.
  • Add a sign by the door or in the window that says gift cards are available.
  • Have staff mention them at checkout through December. One sentence is enough.
  • Tell your regulars by email or on social media.
  • Keep envelopes next to the cards so the gift is ready to hand over.

Restaurants can add a line to the menu or a table tent, since diners are already sitting there with time to read. I also print menus and table tents to match your cards. Spas and salons can hand a card to every client with their receipt in December as a reminder.

Doing both

A lot of businesses sell plastic cards at set values for the holiday rush and keep numbered paper certificates for custom amounts, packages and raffle donations. Paper certificates make a good donation for school and church fundraisers too, and they bring new people through the door. If you also want loyalty cards, a plastic punch card can share the same design so everything matches. You can see more ideas for restaurants and food businesses on our food and beverage page.
